utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday, November 21st, 2007. Good morning, Mr. Scott. Good morning to the Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else assisting the Trial Chamber. In a few minutes we'll have the witness brought in, but I believe somebody wanted to address the Chamber. No one asked to take the floor? No? Well, in that case we'll move into closed session. Let's draw the blinds.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let me remind you that Ms. Nozica has one hour and 45 minutes. Mr. Scott, how much time will you need for redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, I would like to allow for the possibility that I will take one session, one court session. Between breaks is what I mean. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is rather excessive. I don't see how they can manage to get so much time for redirect. I would certainly want to know in advance some justification for that amount of time instead of just going forward with it and granting them and seeing how it goes. What are the topics that they need to cover? What are the documents that they need to go to that will take an entire section for redirect. We have gone through this entire trial where redirect has taken 30 minutes, 40 minutes, but now at this point in time given this evidence, I don't see -- and given the amount of time that they've had for direct examination, I don't see how redirect, because that's going to require perhaps on our part asking for re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott -- yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Through, Your Honour. The Petkovic Defence we support that, strictly speaking of course, provided that the questions do genuinely arise out of cross-examination, then within reason, Your Honours should permit Mr. Scott to continue, but Mr. Karnavas's point is well made, Your Honour, and what we invite is for Your Honours to be particularly rigorous in relation to this matter and not simply allow straying outside the proper ambit of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you are asking for an hour and a half. That would be a record, because so far no -- we haven't ever seen so much time spent on redirect, but my fellow Judge tells me that we've never had so far a cross-examination that took so long. That's true. But still, I believe that Mr. Stewart has spelled out the problem very clearly. In other words, the questions you put during redirect have to be directly connected to the questions put during cross-examination. In other words, you will spend an hour and a half dealing with topics that have already been answered but that you find slightly unsatisfactory. So in other words, you want to re-examine the witness based on the answers he gave during cross-examination. Is that what you intend to do, Mr. Scott? You're not going to broach any new issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, thank you for considering our request. Your Honour, I've been conducting redirect examinations for the best part of 30 years now so I know a little bit about conducting redirect and what the rules of redirect are. As the Court just observed a few minutes ago, this has been by far the longest witness and Defence were allowed ten hours, approximately ten hours. The Prosecution took something around six, and I think that given the extensive cross-examination, no complaint from us where it is relevant the record will show that my interventions through the Defence cross-examinations have been extremely limited. I think yesterday I was only on my feet just a very small number of times and I do know about redirect, and in this particular case, given this witness, given the number of issues that have been raised during cross-examination I think it might, it might take an hour and a half to complete the redirect. Of course, if I can do it more quickly, I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Is the witness here? I'd like to ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Good morning, Ms. Kosta. As you know, we're going to proceed today with your cross-examination. I'm going to give the floor to Ms. Nozica. She has one hour and 45 minutes to complete her cross-examination. Yes. Yes, sir? You've raised your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we begin our work, I would like to request, if possible, and I think that you have the power to do so, that in the transcript a change be made, and instead of the name Viktor Andric which was mentioned fairly frequently yesterday, as well as my other name, Kovac, that my initials, my pseudonym be entered, EA, because should it go public in any way, then it will be no problem to recognise who those names actually refer to. So for my protection. That is my request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges of the Trial Chamber will in any case meet this afternoon, so we'll consider your request, and we'll issue a ruling. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My name is Senka Nozica, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic. I appear together with Mr. Karim Khan sitting setting next to me in the courtroom. You have had a chance to look at my binder. My only wish was that you could take a look at the documents beforehand so that I could get through my job quicker, and I'd like to start off by discussing an area which you also discussed during the examination-in-chief when you gave responses to the Prosecution, and I'd like to go through them and see whether they were wholly true and correct and whether you remember the situations correctly. It refers to the distribution of salaries to the army in Kiseljak, and you said that the salaries were -- or, rather, that the resources to pay out the salaries were received from Grude. I'd like to go through some documents that you've already seen that was shown to you by the Prosecutor and some documents which you have not had an opportunity of seeing until you arrived here. Just to remind you, to refresh your memory, and to see whether that was really how it was or whether the political structures and military structures in Kiseljak --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I wrong or is the transcript not working? Does there seem to be a technical problem? Shall I stop, pause, check? Yes, it is working on the LiveNote. It wasn't working on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll try and refresh your memory and I'll ask you after doing so if you remember in what way from the beginning of the war, so we're speaking of the summer of 1992, right up to, let's say, 1993, whether the salaries were distributed to soldiers in Kiseljak. And in order to do that, let's look at 2D 00570 first. It is the fourth document in my binder, but you can, of course, also wait for it to appear in e-court and on your screen. But I'll start off anyway and you can tell me when you've found it so that we can move on. As I said it was the fourth document from the top.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. It's a protocol from the meeting of the Croatian Defence Ministry, Presidency of the Vares municipality, and the meeting was held on the 26th of January, 1993, and attending the meeting, let's see if you know these people, they were the vice-president of the HVO Mr. Zvonimir Dugonjic; members of the Presidency, Miroslav Pejcinovic, Vladimir Dugonjic, and Ivica Gavran; commander of the Bobovac HVO Brigade Emil Harah; the second in command, Mijo Vukancic; the chief of security, Zvonko Duznovic; and the commander of the 1st Manoeuvre Battalion Marcel Dusper. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to point to certain parts, certain excerpts from the meeting, what they said, so under number 1 we have there what Mr. Zvonimir Dugonjic said, he was the vice-president of the HVO, just to remind you of that. And the second sentence in the first paragraph reads as follows: "The soldiers from Borovica are asking for a salary of 100 Deutschmarks, and objectively speaking, we don't have the means to pay that out. Of course, the authorities will see that -- try and see that there is an increase to -- of the salaries of the troops and that that continues in the future." And now I'd like to read on: "The army is asking that the salary be 30 per cent higher than the civilian authorities, but the military views that in a linear fashion and does not take into consideration job loss, but in contrast to the soldiers from Borovica, the troops at Zabrezje -- we can talk to the troops in Zabrezje because they're more objective." Now, Mr. Harah, in the next paragraph, mentions Kiseljak, so I'll read that out. He says: "I'm not familiar -- I don't know who promised the troops 5.000 Croatian dinars per day spent on the battlefield. I personally talked to the soldiers from the PD platoon who asked for 5 to 10 Deutschmarks or 4.000 Croatian dinars. They mentioned the case of Kiseljak where soldiers receive 10 Deutschmarks for every day spent on the battlefield. I could not make any promises because objectively I would not be able to fulfil them, but in future, I will do my best to see that the pay is as objective as possible and commensurate with the time spent on the battlefield. I said that the HVO Presidency will also get involved to secure more objective pay." Now, I'm going to show you -- or, rather, draw your attention to page 3 of the text in the Croatian version, and it is the first paragraph of the English text. I'll read it out. Miroslav Pejcinovic is speaking, and he says -- well, they were discussing whether catering establishments should be closed down because the troops were drinking too much and Mr. Pejcinovic says: "We can call for the shutting down of the catering establishments, the bars, but how then can we secure salaries for the troops when we know that the largest portion of the financial resources is gained from taxes?" Can you remember, sir, whether this was the way in which the army, not the active duty soldiers but the army was in Kiseljak previously or during that time or later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and answer that by taking the example of Kiseljak, and then I'll go on to comment about what you've just read out. In 1992, until the brigades were established, and while the Municipal Staffs functioned, the HVO formations, units, were generally worked on a voluntary basis. That's how they functioned. And during that time there was a certain amount of financing from the municipal budgets in the way that you described it, as was read out here. There was money coming into the budget for financing the army and also from the budget of the municipal structures. I cannot claim that during that period in -- of time that the salaries from Herzegovina -- or, rather, from Grude, as I said, came regularly and that they came in proportion to the number of soldiers deployed. Certain monies did arrive, which then in keeping with how much the soldiers and officers took part in certain military activities we would distribute that money to them proportionately. But that wasn't on a regular basis either. That was just from time to time, because we couldn't count on receiving money every month. But I would also agree with the observation that the municipal structures, the municipal organs, also collected resources in this way in order to finance the HVO. Now, when we speak about the ten mark per day stimulation, while the HVO was based on the principle of volunteers, voluntary work, it was difficult to order anybody to go to the battlefront in Jajce, for example, or later on to Travnik. Afterwards we found a solution and we said well, for every day spent on the battlefield we're going to stimulate that work by paying out ten Deutschmarks. So that money was collected from the municipal authorities, organs. Later on when the brigades were established, as far as I remember in Kiseljak there was no further intervention in that sense. That is to say that money had to be paid in for the salaries. But if there were any problems with the money coming in from Herzegovina, then we would ask for loans. We would pay the soldiers their salaries, and once we received our salaries from Herzegovina we would pay back those funds. And I would like to mention that there were cases, as you were able to see, that I asked they be remunerated for certain military activities. And so in cases of that kind the money was paid out from the municipal pile. The municipal cash-box.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you received resources from Grude during a period of time but that you distributed it to all the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The criteria were determined in the command, how they were to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you remember that they came in for the active-duty officers? That's what you've said, but you wanted the regular soldiers to receive something too so you distributed those resources. Can you remember anything along those lines referring to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the resources did come in, and we treated them as money for salaries, but it was left up us to decide what criteria we were going to use to distribute them, but we decided to use the linear method so that the soldiers would not be dissatisfied, so that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, this additional explanation you've just given us that the resources for the salaries, the money for the salaries and for the active-duty soldiers didn't arrive on a regular basis. Now, the first document, and it was shown by the Prosecutor as well, it's in the Prosecution's binder, it's a short -- a short document and it will come up on e-court. The number is P 05915. Do you have the Prosecution binder? Perhaps you'll need it in a while, so it would be a good idea to have it with you. Ah, now the document's come up on e-court. Take a look at it, sir. This is a request for information about salaries for soldiers under contract, and the military police. You signed it. You sent it to the assistant commander for logistics, the finance office, on the 16th of October, 1993, and in the sirs again sense there, that is to say in October 1993, you say the following: "Please explain in brief, by giving a brief answer, what the chances are of soldiers under contract in the Maturice and Apostoli PPN, Special Purpose Unit, receive salaries since they are entitled to them under their contracts." Now, reading this paragraph and thinking about it logically from this document of ours, I can conclude that they did not receive salaries up until then, because you're asking for an answer, and -- and you're asking it in October 1993, for the possibility of them being paid salaries. Now, you go on to say: "Also, please inform us if it is possible for members of the military police to receive at least a lump sum by way of financial assistance so that they should not think of abusing their position and authority." Now, logically, sir, reading through this, and please try and remember, I hope it refreshes your memory, we can conclude that the military police, that is to say members of the brigade military police, that's what we're talking about, they, too, did not receive regular salaries, and that the Maturice and Apostoli did not either, and you're looking into the possibility of resolving that problem. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is this: There were cases when the salaries came in very late, sometimes two months, sometimes even three months. They were three months late. And on the ground that presented a problem because people had to live off something, and they were engaged and deployed all the time. So this document of mine describes that situation, says that the salaries were being paid out late and that people wanted to have those rights fulfilled. So I wanted to have this situation solved, and that's why I wanted to speed it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, this is called request. The document is called a request.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try and slow down. So you're looking into ways and means of speeding the process up and having the salaries paid out, and you mentioned a situation where you decided on the financial remuneration. So let's link that up to a document, and it is this document, P 07757. And you said in that document, 07757, that the remuneration was paid from the municipal money, the municipal money. Am I right looking at this document on e-court now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We'll move on to another area. This is an area that could be called your relationship with the Serbs, not to use the word "cooperation." We will look into that. We will look at some documents. Did you or the HVO during that period of time cooperate with the Serbs or were you actually forced to have contacts with them in order to survive, and those contacts were actually conditioned, if we may call it so. You were actually blackmailed in order to obtain certain means that you could not obtain in any other way. His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you when Mr. Praljak showed you a map of Kiseljak, Judge Antonetti asked you whether you, in 1992 and 1993, in Kiseljak were encircled and you answered that you were. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that in 1992 we were not encircled, but we came under such a situation towards the end of January 1993 after the conflicts in Central Bosnia between the HVO and the BiH army. From then on until the end of the war, one may say that Kiseljak was encircled by the Muslim forces. We only had one point of contact, some couple of kilometres long, with the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely what you answered to the Judge. You said from the moment of the initial conflict with the Muslim side you were encircled, and that would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: During that period of time the answer seems to be logical, but I'm still going to ask you. During that period of time were you able to receive any weapons, I'm talking about weapons only, from the logistical base in Grude if it didn't go through the Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about the time when I returned to Kiseljak, which was the beginning of April and onwards towards the end of the war. I can confirm that there was no other possibility for us to receive anything that was necessary for combat and defence of the territory of Kiseljak if it didn't go through the territory of -- that was under the control of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Generally speaking, can you tell us what was the military situation when you had your initial contacts with the Serbs? Would it be correct to conclude that your initial contacts with the Serbs actually started during the BiH offensives against the areas of Kakanj, Fojnica, and Kiseljak in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our contacts with the Serb side started before my arrival in Kiseljak, and I provided some documents, speaking about that. If you want to know any details, I will gladly give you some. When the fighting stepped up in Central Bosnia, when the Kakanj fell and when the fighting intensified around Kiseljak and Vitez, there was no other possibility. Depending on the situation that contact and that cooperation, so to speak, with the Serbs, would intensify from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what was the interest on the part of the Serb to have the Croats remain in Vares? What was their military interest to see them remain in Vares?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contact, i.e., the area where the Bobovac Brigade and the municipality of Vares was in contact with the Serb side was quite a large area. If the Croats from Vares, i.e., the Bobovac Brigade had left the area, the Serb side would have needed a large number of men, a lot of equipment in order to close that area off and that was not in their best interest. They did not want to see the Bobovac Brigade leave the area, because they did not have enough manpower to protect the area. They did not have the equipment. Actually, they did have the equipment, but they didn't have enough manpower to defend that area. Their interest was purely military interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that as a matter of fact the military interest of the Serbs very often dictated what they would give to you, what they would say to you, how they would sell it to you? We're talking about various equipment and military support. Their priority was always their own military interest; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please. In my binder you saw some documents and we are going to talk about some concrete -- the prices that you paid for the things that you bought from the Serbs, but in general terms let me ask you, what kind of prices are we talking about? Were they more or less the same or similar to the market prices, or were you blackmailed by the Serbs who imposed their prices upon you because you didn't have a choice, because you -- they knew that you were not in a position to obtain the arms in any other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm going to object to the use of the word "blackmail." I think it's inappropriate in this instance and I think it's just inflammatory language by counsel. They chose to cooperate with the Serbs to obtain needed weapons, no question about that but to say they were blackmailed is a bit like saying that I'm blackmailed because I have to come to court every day because it's my job. In that way I'm being blackmailed to come to court. I think it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you used the word of "cooperation" and now you're using the word "blackmail." It's not exactly the same thing. Mr. Scott is absolutely right. Please rephrase your question differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will repeat my question, but I would like to explain why I used the term that I did. If somebody asks a lot more for a thing than this thing actually costs and that person knows that you are forced to buy that thing from them, then I believe that the term that I used was right, but let me ask the witness whether the prices that they paid were much higher than the prices that were on the marketplace at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I get the point, but that's basically somebody who's trying to take advantage of the favourable situation in order to charge higher prices. It's something that happens in an economic situation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, just as someone who was taught criminal law all his life say that what you mean is probably usury, "usure," taking advantage of a position of inferiority to ask excessive prices is called "wucher" in German, "usure" in French, I think "usury" in English. And that would then be something that one can discuss. I actually do not think that the word "chantage," "blackmail," in this context is legally what you actually mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point I was not speaking in legal terms. I was just talking about the facts that existed on the ground. In any case, I would like to thank the honourable Judge Antonetti for explaining things in legal terms. But let's forget the term that I originally used. When the Trial Chamber renders their decision, they will decide whether it was cooperation or something else, but they will decide that after they have analysed the elements that went into that contact or cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you have not answered my question. Let's go back to it. Tell me whether the prices that you paid were much higher sometimes than would have been paid elsewhere and whether those prices were as high as they were because that was the only way for you to obtain those weapons, because you didn't have any other means to obtain them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here a legal question has developed but allow me to say a couple of sentence about that because I was there. I know. The Serbs obviously knew, they monitored the situation that we were in, and their requests and their demands with regard to the prices and our demands were mostly in line with their information about the situation that we were in at that moment. If they knew the -- what we were asking was -- was absolutely indispensable, then their demands were higher because they knew that we would give in. They also demanded us to put a stop to some combat activities in the north of Bosnia where Muslims and Croats teamed up against the Serbs in order for them to give us a concession in Central Bosnia in terms of a convoy or delivery of weapons. As far as prices are concerned, those prices ranged from five times to ten times more than the prices were on the market. We used any possible way or means to get hold of fighting equipment. I was familiar with that, I approved those things. I did whatever I could in order to save our people and the area that I was in charge of, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now we're going to look at some documents that I have prepared to see whether the situation was the way you describe it. This is now a Prosecutor's document which will appear on e-court. The document number is P 02973. Just for the record, I would like to say that in the binder we have a document P 02966. This is the same document, just to avoid any future confusion. Please look at the document. The document has already been shown to you by the Prosecutor. As far as I can remember, the date is 26th June, 1993. Can we conclude that this was the period when the fighting in the area of Central Bosnia intensified against the BiH army? Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say here and you say to yourself that they are offering you a certain number of rifles at a price of 5.000 German marks, and you asked for the price not to exceed 1.000 German marks. You yourself at that moment estimated that regardless of your position, that price was much higher than any normal price. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This price of 1.000 German marks for this type of weapon is also high, but I was willing and ready at that moment to pay that much, but I could not accept the price of 5.000 German marks. That was just excessive.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, then. The next document, you will recognise it. P 09965. I believe that you yourself provided it to the OTP. This document was issued on the 6th of July, 1993. You send information about your contact with the XY side. You sent it to the chief of the Main Staff and to the head of the defence department. Let's wait for the document to appear on e-court. Have you received the Prosecutor's binder in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have a problem with the documents appearing on e-court. The number is 09965. This should be towards the end of the binder. This is not the Prosecutor's document. As far as I can remember, this is Ms. Alaburic's document in her orange binder. The usher does not have his headphones on so he can't hear what I'm saying. I hope you have been provided with two binders. It should be in the second binder. 9965 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is already open. It is before your eyes, Mr. EA.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can see it on e-court. Just now it has appeared on e-court. But we're still waiting for the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in front of me in the original version.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, then. I would like to show you the second page of this document which is the most important for our whole story, to show the situation that you were in. On page 2 you say: "As you know, we lack things. Some of the things have been reduced to zero." You are listing the things that you don't have, bullets of different calibre. Does it arise from this document quite indisputably that at that moment you were in a rather desperate situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, then. Can we please look at the following document as far as I can understand it should be in first Prosecutor's binder, the number is P 03403, that's the number of the document, P 03403. Yes. While you're looking for it, let me remind you that this is another letter of yours dated 12 July 1993, which you sent to the president of the HZ HB, the head of the defence department and also to the chief of the Main Staff. In this document you're again speaking about your contact with the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't have the document before me. I don't have it either in the original hard copy or in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P 03403. We have been having a lot of problems this morning. I suppose we will take some time to warm up which is consuming a lot of my time. Have you got it now? Have you got it on e-court? Thank you. Brilliant. I'm going to refer you to the middle portion of the documents. You're familiar with your document. You're saying: "We're receiving the artillery support only in the places where their positions are threatened in objective terms. Where a situation is the hardest for us this is beyond their range." Does this explain the kind of cooperation you had with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. You have just mentioned that you were blackmailed by the Serbs, that they would give you support if you put a stop to the fighting that you conducted jointly with the BH army in some parts of the Bosnia against the Serbs. Could you please look at document P 03460. I believe that this is the document that illustrates your claim. The number is P 03460. Here you say, and this is another report: "We inform you that the convoy with the materiel, equipment, food and personnel that was prepared in Grude and should have been transported to Kiseljak through the territory of XY with the approval of the XY side did not get the approval with the explanation that the members of the Croatian army, as they say, are opening fire at our forces in Posavina." This is a cry given the situation in Central Bosnia on the 15th of July, 1993, and it is only logical, and if you can agree with me you are saying here, "We're asking you to react urgently to order to save what can be saved for we have only a critical minimum of MTS and food."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't want to interrupt. I was just waiting for counsel to finish the question. As I mentioned at the outset this morning I have tried to on the cross-examination of this witness to really intervene on a minimal basis but I have to intervene on the same point before. Counsel, for some reason, really wants to call this blackmail and again on page 20, line 14, "Well, you have just mentioned that you were blackmailed by the Serbs ..." Now, the witness didn't say that, but counsel persists in wanting to characterise it in that way. That's just simply not the case, and unfortunately, counsel continues --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me counsel if counsel continues to do that, I will have to continue to intervene. Now, what's happening here, Your Honour, is that there is no dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence, seemingly, on this point. There was extensive cooperation between the Croats and the Serbs in this area. They were renting tanks. They were renting artillery. They were helping each other out to their mutual interest. The Serbs took advantage of the situation to get some more money. There is no dispute about that. The parties are in agreement. But you know what's happening really is that even now, even now our accused can't help to say that they extensively cooperated with the Serbs so they want to say we were blackmailed. There was extensive ongoing, almost day-to-day, cooperation with the Serbs in this area. No dispute about that. But it's not blackmail.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, if you will allow me, I have not used the word "blackmail." All who speak Croatian in this courtroom can confirm that. But there is dispute between the Prosecution and Defence whether this was cooperation, and what I'm trying to do now in my cross-examination is to contest the Prosecution's claim that that cooperation existed on a voluntary basis, because a contact between the two sides does not imply, either in logical terms or in legal terms, cooperation. I understand why my learned friend Mr. Scott has intervened on several occasions, but I have not used the word "blackmail," and if you allow me, I will continue, and the -- and the Judge will -- the Judges will decide whether this was blackmail indeed or something else, or cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Without going into the subject matter, I would only like to say that in the English translation it was mentioned that "blackmail," blackmailing. So even at the very last moment when Mr. Scott raised. So therefore the English translation contained the word "blackmail." It is what I would like to say. Furthermore, let me ask your witness EA not to answer immediately after the questions. You are always interrupting, actually, the translation, and you start speaking, of course, in the Croat. And let me ask you to wait and to pause. Imandana [phoen]. And you have time and you can do that after one minute of waiting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica, please continue. But we do have a problem, or at least in the interpretation. We see the word "blackmail." It means blackmail. Now, what was the word that you used in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, I'd have to listen to everything I said. I can't say. But I did take care not to use the word "ucijena" again, but I will try to take care of that in future.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, look at the document, please, sir, so that we can practically -- in practical terms see what Judge Trechsel said when he -- when Mr. Praljak was asking the questions. The difference in prices. Let's have a look at that, and let's have a look at the Prosecution document. It is P 09967. Tell me when you've found it, because that's important. It should be in the second Prosecution binder, but it seems to me that you're having a lot of difficulty in finding your way around, and you don't seem to have the binder at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why the witness hasn't got the binder. It just makes the proceedings slower. The Prosecutor has a lot of time, but I don't, unfortunately, and I have two significant areas to deal with, and this is slowing up my cross-examination quite an a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I am quite convinced that the document will appear on e-court quickly, and I'll tell you what it's about. It's your letter dated the 5th of November, 1993, which you sent to Bruno Stojic in person, addressed personally to him, and you put the proposal forward of the Serb side about prices and the calculation of cost. Here we have the prices. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. Now, under number 2 we have prices for ammunition, et cetera, and then some other pieces, and at the end of the document you say -- or, rather, you request that an answer be sent quickly and that the prices and criteria will be resolved at the level of the government and that Colonel Kljajic can just sign for what they received and when they began using the equipment. I'm sure you will remember the prices. I'll just go on to the second and third document and we'll come back to this one. Now take a look at document P 9820 in your binder. It should be a document in front of the one we've been looking at. Could you just confirm that that was the answer from Mr. Bruno Stojic to your letter, a response to your letter. It's come up on e-court. Do you agree that that is indeed what I said it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is Mr. Stojic's answer to your letter. Now, in my binder take a look at the tenth document. It is 2D 577, 00577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Before the witness looks at the document, I would like to know the following: Witness, Mr. Stojic sends you a letter on the 6th of November. In this letter it seems that he states that following a meeting between the Government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the Government of Republika Srpska, a harmonisation took place, or they have reached a harmonisation concerning materiel and so on. Now, when you received this document, what is your opinion of it? Did you think that, politically speaking, an agreement had been reached between Herceg-Bosna and Republika Srpska on this matter of weapons, of prices, and materiel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot say that a political agreement was reached, but I can describe to you what the situation was like and that I used this document. It was useful to me to send on to the other side to inform them of the position of my superiors and to say that the problems would be solved at the level as has been explained here to me, and that I was not authorised to discuss prices. And after this kind of answer, I would receive some concession from the Serb side, because this was a guarantee that it would be resolved, in fact, at a higher level. Now, whether there was a political agreement or military agreement I would refrain from stating either way because I didn't attend the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, would you now take a look -- have you found the document that I told you, 2D 00577?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sure you looked at the document overnight as well. It is dated the 23rd of December, 1992. It is a document sent by the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council to Travnik and he's sending it to the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, from this document we can see that the HVO had in its area, on its territory, a weapons factory which was known as BNT, but that was short for Bratstvo Novi Travnik, Brotherhood Novi Travnik, and there was an agreement that was being implemented and should continue to be implemented between the BH army and the HVO for the replenishment of MTS from this factory, materiel and technical equipment. So, did you know that? And we're referring to December, that an agreement like this existed and that the goods produced by this factory was distributed equally to both sides on the basis of an agreement? So it was in fact an agreement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time there were agreements like that, and it was something that was acted upon. I cannot say how much, to what extent. I wasn't a participant, but I do know that such activities were underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, that's why this document is important, but it also served me to see what on the 23rd of December, 1992, the situation was like and the price was of artillery pieces or weapons when they were sold for realistic economic prices, economically formed prices. Now, I'd just like to draw your attention to a minor point -- or, rather, I don't consider it to be a minor point. I consider it to be very important. The first table in this document where it says how things were distributed, and we come to artillery pieces, the H77 Oganj, a very important piece of equipment. Just one such artillery piece was distributed to the BH army. It's on page 00594472 of the English -- or, rather, in the English version it doesn't say that. That's been left out. So it appears that this piece called Oganj, the M77 Oganj was one that nobody received. It's been left out. Now let's look at the next table. It's page 3 of your document, in fact. And in the English translation it is the last table. And here we have the prices of what we call MTS. And then after that we have a table which once again says a review of the equipment delivered, and we have the cost of each individual artillery piece. Now, if I wish to compare this with the prices that the Serbs sent -- sold you, or the HVO weapons, I prepared in all the binders, including your own, at the end of the binder an extra document, an additional document. And now, if possible, may we have on e-court -- may we have a document back? It is P 09967. Back on e-court, please. P 09967. And you have the last document with the prices in front of you. That's your own document. So we can compare the prices. I'll try and do that as quickly as possible. P 09967. Page 1, please, the first page, on e-court. In your document, the one you signed and sent to Mr. Bruno Stojic, under number 2 you have the price and cost of bullets, ammunition, bullets and mines, and the mine -- the price of mines is -- for 82 millimetres is 570 Deutschmarks. Now, in this table that you have in front of you, you have those same mines under number 5, and the price there is 67 Deutschmarks; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that, but I don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's in the Prosecution binder. P 09967. We seem to have a problem. P 09967. When you find it, you can compare it to my document. So this mine which is in the table, the last table in the English, it's the 82-millimetre one, and the offer there by the Serbs was 570 Deutschmarks, and here, number 5, we see -- it says an inert mine, and it only costs 67 Deutschmarks there. Now let's look at the 120-millimetre mine. It was offered -- they were offering it to you at a price of 2.800 Deutschmarks, and in the other table the price there, number 6, is 302 marks. Right? Number 6.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got your document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My document is in my binder, and the number is 2D 577. It is the tenth document from the top, the tenth in order, and it's the letter we analysed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you should be looking at the table that I'm referring to now. It's the first table -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. We can continue now. Let me repeat. The 120-millimetre mine was being offered to you by the Serbs for 2.800 Deutschmarks, whereas in my table, my document, it is number 6, and the price there is 302 Deutschmarks. Now let's take a 122-millimetre bullet as another example. The price there is 2.520 Deutschmarks. That's what the Serbs were offering. And under number 11 in my document, that bullet costs 450 Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, just leaf through my document or go on a page, and it is the penultimate page in the English version. It is the table for certain artillery pieces. So let's take a look at that. Let's look at number 1. It is an MD -- MB 120. The Serbs are asking 50.000 for that, 50.000 Deutschmarks. And that artillery piece in the other table is under 1, and the price there is 13.961 marks. Other artillery pieces coincide. For example, the MB 88-millimetre one. On the Serb offer, the realistic price is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's not spend more time on this. We saw when you compared the prices that the prices vary from 3 to 10, but please get to the important questions. It's not -- there's no doubt about it that there are some price differences. So if the Judges -- the Judges will look at these pages and we'll be able to compare the prices by themselves. So please get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly what I was trying to do. I was trying to show by way of documents what Judge Trechsel put to the witness as a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, can you agree that these prices that are indicated in the documents are the prices that were determined at the arms factory in -- factory as the prices that would have been realistic on the marketplace if you hadn't been in the situation that you were in and if you hadn't been in a position to provide those arms at much higher prices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time those were objective weapons prices.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now look at document P 06217.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica. Witness, on these tables that we -- we -- that the Defence has put forward, we have a column with the prices, and then next to it we have a column which is entitled "Value," and which also translates the items listed, mortars, ammunition, and so forth, into a figure which normally is enormously higher than the price, which to an observer suggests that these produces that were domestically produced were priced below value, but I may be completely wrong in this. Can you explain? Does this make sense to you, and could you tell us which sense it makes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it would seem that the answer is extremely simple. The value column is the result of the multiplication of the amount of pieces and the price. If you take number 1, we take 85 multiplied by 3.361 and so on and so forth, and 2 times 300 is 6000. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at the -- the document P 06217. That's the next document that I would like you to look at. We have it on e-court let's just go through this document very briefly because I have used up a lot of my time already. This is your document that you sent on the 28th of October, 1993, to various addresses mentioning a meeting with the minister of health of Republika Srpska, Mr. Dragan Kalinic, and you state that you still owe something for certain medical services provided to you and you are saying in the bottom part of the document with the purpose of settling these claims, the Serbian side can accept the following options and the Serb side is now asking for heating fuels for hospitals, fuel for motor vehicles, medical -- medical equipment and medicines in accordance with the specifications as well as cash. Sir, can you please explain to the Trial Chamber why did the soldiers or why did you in Kiseljak in the encirclement use the services of the war hospital of Republika Srpska in Blazuj? Did you have any other possibility of sending citizens or soldiers anywhere else for treatment or was this the only possibility that you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time when we were encircled in Kiseljak we did not have a hospital that would be able to deal with more serious cases when it came to various war wounds and injuries. And since we maintained contact with the Serb side, we were allowed passage to their hospital. We were forced to use their services, to ask them for assistance, and they would provide it to us under the conditions as described herein. They would provide us with those services; they would treat our wounded. Their hospital was much better equipped. That was their war hospitals. They had instruments, they had the personnel, and they provided services to us under the conditions as described herein.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, then. Just briefly let's have a look at 2D 583 in my binder, which is the third document from the bottom of the list. I'm sure that you have already had a look at that document, which is quite extensive, and I don't have the time to go through all of it. Please alert me when you have located that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, this is the invoice for treated HVO soldiers and civilians from the territory of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. This document contains as a compilation of those invoices, i.e., this is a payment document testifying to the payments, and the price list of certain services. Do you remember that you actually paid these invoices, and do you remember that you had a price list for every service that was provided to you, i.e., to the citizens and soldiers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this document originates from the war hospital and refers to the communication with my headquarters, with my superior command and further on, and I do remember these documents, and this is exactly what we did and how this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At the end I would like to ask you with regard to all of these documents and I have just one more document that we have to look at. Can these documents fully confirm what you said at the beginning, and that was that you were forced to maintain contacts with the Serbs, first of all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not have a choice. We did not have any other solution. There was a -- an alternative solution and that was to use helicopter evacuation of the wounded to Herzegovina or even further afield. If we -- if that was not available to us in order to save the lives of the people who were wounded, we did not have a choice. You had to save those people. You did not give it a second thought as to who would provide that service to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. My question was this: You were forced to main that -- maintain that contact with the Serbs because of the situation that you were in, and I am implying the supply of the MTS, the passage of convoys, and the treatment of citizens and soldiers of the HVO. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Not a single one of those services, if you can call them that, not a single one of the service that were provided to you by the Serbs was free of charge. Was that -- was -- would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They charged and each service had a price.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you -- when you say they had a price, does that mean that sometimes you paid in cash, sometimes in oil, and sometimes in the produce that the HVO had and the Serbs were lacking; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we then say that the conditions and the ways of payment were mostly dictated by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They imposed their conditions and payments were done at a high level. I was not familiar with the way things had been negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You're saying that they imposed their conditions, and if those conditions were accepted then you would have been provided with the services or the goods. And when I say you, I mean generally speaking. If the HVO accepted the conditions, then you would be provided with what was agreed. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we go briefly back to document number P 60 -- I apologise. P 06267 is the correct number of the document. I believe that this document was used on direct and that this document caused some misunderstanding. The number is P 06267. This is a Prosecutor's document. You have it on e-court at the moment. I am going to ask you several questions that arise from the questions put to you by Judge Antonetti with regard to this document. The Judge asked you whether this was an order sent to you by Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please. Before you put a question regarding convoys, I would like to go back to the previous question. We saw some documents in which we saw that the Serbs would charge you for medical help in their hospitals. Did you have your own soldiers, for instance, that were injured and that you would send to a Serb hospital, and did you have to pay for the services? Let's say your injured soldiers, were they actually taken care of in those hospitals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My own brother was among them, and a large number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You answered my first question. Now second question: By looking at the document, I saw that for HVO soldiers we saw that there was a mention, but also for civilians. I would like to know if when it comes to civilians that went to those Serb hospitals, are those Croatian civilians, Muslim civilians, Serb civilians? To your knowledge, who are these civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those civilians hailed from the territory of Kiseljak, Kresevo, and Fojnica, and they were mostly Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Last question. When they would go there, they would have to go through lines that were controlled by the Serbs. So how was that done, through telephone contacts or messages? Was there a procedure that was put in place according to which these people could go cross the lines and go to the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In Kiseljak we would have to issue them a written -- written permit to be able to cross to the other side, and in agreement with the Serb side when that person would appear on their side with our document, our piece of paper giving permission to them, then they would let him go where he had set out for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I imagine that the people who were severely injured were transported by ambulance. I imagine that there were ambulance that would go from point A to point B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And tell me, the international community that was present in Kiseljak, they knew of all of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, sir, can we clarify this question of the international community. Since we both come from that region, can we conclude that at those check-points or the border between Croatia -- or, rather, the HVO and the Serb side, that there were mostly vehicles belonging to international organisations, and they conducted regular control and supervision of who was crossing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say they were regular, but that they were passing by there and that they did have many of their members communicating along that line and could see that going on, I don't challenge that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we have another document that I wanted to ask you something about before the break just briefly, and that is a letter sent to you from Mr. Bruno Stojic. Judge Antonetti asked you whether you received this order. Let's clear that up first. Is this an order at all, or is it just a letter which you were supposed to convey to Minister Kovacevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Koravacevic"] via courier, send on to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, tell me, this letter not have to read it out again, does it in fact represent a request for agreement for the passage of the convoy, for the convoy to pass through? Read it and tell me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Perhaps it's just a mistake in the transcript whether it is military units passing by or the transport of military units or transportation units as it says here, trucks, cars, or anything that is considered a transportation unit. Right? It says the convoy would be made up of eight transportation units. Now, that's a simple question. Does that imply -- mean cars and vehicles, or does it mean military unit manpower?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is something not quite satisfactory in the transcript, and I would direct your attention to page 36, line 9. "The question is is this an order at all, or is it just a letter which you were supposed to convey to Minister Koravacevic." Kovacevic, it should probably be. And the answer is yes. Now, either/or question is not really answered by yes, so perhaps, Ms. Nozica, you want to recall and get that clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. And my colleague has just drawn my attention to that, that there is a slight confusion there in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So let me ask you, is this an order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is it a letter that you were supposed to send on to Mr. Kovacevic or, rather, Minister Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I think we've cleared up this matter of the transport or transportation units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, as I understand it not this letter is to be transferred to the Minister Kovacevic but, rather, a document in which this free passage is granted. Is it not so? Do I misunderstand this? The letter says: "Please issue approval for the passage," and I think this approval should then be sent by courier to Minister Kovacevic. Maybe I misunderstand this completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do believe you have misunderstood it. Might I be allowed to explain this to you and the witness is listening so he can confirm if I'm right in what I'm going to say. It says here, or rather, this letter requests approval for the passage of convoys and then in capital letters at the end it says: "Send the document at once to Minister Kovacevic via courier," which means this document, the document which Mr. -- is the one that Mr. EA should have sent on -- should send on to Mr. Kovacevic, because it is a request for approval for passage or permission for the passage of convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that, Mr. EA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do not use the name if possible. We have to redact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I do apologise. I knew I had to make a mistake somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now just one question before the break, sir. Did you ever hear when you were at liberty or anywhere else that this man, Mr. Kovacevic, who was the minister, whether he was accused of war crimes, a suspect of having committed war crimes or anything similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps that would be a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take a break. We have 45 minutes -- you have 45 minutes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just with your permission, just one question to make more sense of this last document. Is it to be understood that this Minister Kovacevic is actually a Serbian or Republika Srpska minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now it's -- thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to apologise to Mr. Scott, the Trial Chamber, the interpreters, and everybody in the courtroom. My client drew my attention to the fact that I repeated the word "blackmail" for the second time. I would like to say that I did it inadvertently, because it seems that in my mind I believe that what was going on was that. That's in the back of my mind, and that's why I used the word, and I apologise for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, we're moving on to another topic. Can you please confirm that the BiH army, approximately in the month of June, attacked Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took Kakanj. The BH army took Kakanj in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I am not insisting on the word militarily attacking. My second question: After the occupation of Kakanj was the civilian population expelled from Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me two sentences. After meeting up with the Prosecutor, we discussed that and I managed to introduce him to the factual basis that the population did not leave the area of their own will, and I would adhere to that. Whether this will be proven differently, whether another qualification will ever be given to that, I wouldn't go into that. This is what I wanted to be entered into the factual base.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, yes. Just for the transcript, I would like to emphasise that this is item 11 of the factual basis. You don't have to start looking for it. I'm sure that everybody in the courtroom will be able to locate it. You're saying that people did not leave of their own will. This is the qualification that corresponds to what you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we also say that the same happened in Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we also say that the BiH army, after Stupni Do, after the events there, attacked Vares and that the people were expelled from that area as well, or as you are putting it, they did not leave of their own will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to put it to you, although I did not intend to dwell upon this for a long time, you're saying that they did not leave of their own will, and I have to ask you this: When it comes to Kakanj, when it comes to Vares, the fact that they did not leave of their own will, was that the consequence of the attack and taking of these places on the part of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is with certainty about Vares because I participated in those events. After the attack of the BiH army on the area of Vares, when the military forces of the HVO withdrew it was only logical that the population would leave the territory together with their army, and it was a normal consequence of everything that had been going on before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any information as to what was happening or what happened to the Croats who remained in Kakanj? Did you have any information about that once the HVO withdrew to a majority of the Croatian population? Do you know what happened to the Croats who decided to remain in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had information, at least as far as I can remember, that moment that a lot of people were detain -- detained in the so-called thermo-electric plant which is a space where people could be kept. There was arson. People got killed, civilians and army members, but I wouldn't be able to go into any details. I don't want to speculate. It was a long time ago and I didn't dwell upon that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Quickly, sir, since the time moves quickly I would like to show you a document about Kakanj it is in my binder, 2D 00568 is the number of the document. I believe it's the second document in my binder.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is information by the Supreme Command of the armed forces. I don't know whether you have ever seen this document before. This is about a progress of combat activities in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the 24-hour period for the day 14 June 1993. This is the report for the 1st corps and 2nd Corps of the BH army. Can we please look at the third page of the document in the Croatian version, which is the penultimate page in the English version as far as I can tell. This is the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, the last paragraph in that bigger section. It says: "Our forces," and this refers to the BiH army forces, of course, "broke HVO, the HVO forces in the Kakanj municipality in a decisive action. This was done by 7th Mountain Brigade in cooperation with the Municipal Staff of Kakanj and the 309th Mountain Brigade." Was this really the case as it was stated herein?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they know what it was like and so they're describing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you confirm that precisely on that day as it says here, the 14th of June, 1993, it happened the way they say it did, that their forces broke the HVO forces -- or, rather, that Kakanj fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, I've prepared quite a number of documents, but I'd like to go on to another area that I consider to be of no lesser importance, and it's the part where you spoke about investigations, alleged investigations -- or, rather, let's move on to the area of Stupni Do. Judge Antonetti asked you yesterday what your duty was, what you were required to do if you learnt that a soldier subordinate to you had committed a war crime, and you said that you would issue an order to your assistant for SIS to conduct an investigation. Is that what you said? Do you remember that? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Similarly, yesterday you said that it was the duty of the assistant for SIS to file a criminal report. We're talking of the assistant for SIS of the brigade or operations group, the person subordinate to you, and that you, as his commanding officer, did not have the duty of undertaking anything further, anything more than that. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense of an investigation, I don't think I had any obligations, but if that SIS person were to ask me to do something additionally which was within my purview and authority, then I should have done that. I would be required to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And if this assistant for SIS did not ask you to do anything, to undertake anything further, then did you have the obligation of checking to see what he had actually done and to see whether he did what you told him to do, the order you gave him, whether he had carried it out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he should have informed me about the substance of the matter -- or, rather, about what he did. So I think, yes, he should have informed me so that I should know what to do in future as a military commander. If I needed to do anything, I would know what to focus on. So he should have reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So from your answer now, I conclude that you should have or must have received feedback information. Let's see this in military terms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the SIS person evaluated what was -- what I should be informed of and what wasn't needed, what I need not have been informed of.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, if the assistant for SIS found that there was reason for -- reason to prosecute and he took steps, would that be an important piece of information that he should have informed you about, that he was required to inform you of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would it be vital if the assistant for SIS found that there were absolutely no grounds or that a crime had not taken place and that he stopped the investigation? So if he had done that, would he have had to have informed you about that too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now -- I apologise to you in advance, Mr. EA, because you answered questions about some legal matters. I know that you're not a lawyer. You have no legal training. But as you gave us some answers yesterday, I really have to ask you some questions on the same topic. Do you know which organ was authorised to conduct an investigation into criminal acts prosecuted along official lines, including the crime of war crimes? Do you know who the sole authorised organ was to conduct an investigation into that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I knew which the sole authorised organ was to conduct an investigation, but I do know that that should have been done along the lines of -- or -- the military police, the military prosecutor's office, and the security service. Now, what remit these parties had in conducting an investigation I really don't know. I can't say. I can't be specific and draw a line.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, I insist upon the word "investigation," which was mentioned yesterday frequently precisely to see what the SIS and military police would have to do and you acting upon somebody's orders. So in the criminal legal sense, it would not be an investigation per se, but it would be some preliminary steps. In layman terms, there is no great difference, but legally there is, and that's why I insist upon it. There's a big difference. I'd like to bring up a document that Ms. Alaburic showed you yesterday, 4D 00861. I'm sure you have the orange binder, her orange binder, and if not, we'll wait for it to come up on e-court. We have it on e-court. May we just zoom in where it says the provision about military district courts, county military courts on the territory. Yes. Or, rather, military district courts on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during -- during war and an immediate threat of war -- or immediate war danger. We have that. I'm asking you about the prosecutor's office now. When it comes to the prosecutor's office, I'd like to draw your attention to Article 3, which says that the County Military Courts, proceedings before the County Military Courts shall be -- come under the competence of the Military District Court when proceedings are taken officially, and necessary measures are taken in detecting, uncovering the crimes and the perpetrators of the crimes, request for undertaking and investigation, raise an indictment, and the appeals. Now, from Article 3 of this decree on the prosecutor's office says that the prosecutor's offices are in charge of conducting an investigation, and under 1 it says, "shall take the necessary measure in uncovering criminal acts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Ms. Nozica. You're quoting Article 3. You've read out the entirety of Article 3. When I'm looking at the English version, it doesn't seem to correspond to Article 3 that you've just read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I have noticed is that on e-court you only have a translation of the decree on military district courts. The other one is P 00947, and I read the article regarding district prosecutors' offices. There is no translation in English there. I can see that. But I've dealt with that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to repeat, witness, you're not a lawyer, but from what it says here, this article, it emerges that it is the prosecutor's office that is the sole organ in charge of conducting an investigation. Now let's look at the courts, district military courts, that provision and decree. We have the translation of that. Ms. Alaburic, on the 19th of November, during her cross-examination she read out Article 25 of this decree. She read it out in total. And in view of your responses to questions put to you about that Article, I'm going to read it again. So for the transcript, Article 25, please, and the answers are on page 83, line 18 to page 84, line 14 of the transcript of the 19th of November, 2007. We have that Article, Article 25, in front us. Mrs. Alaburic asked you the following -- I'll just read it out. In Article 25 it says that in a criminal proceedings before the County Military Courts, applicable law for criminal proceedings that was taken over as a republican law, and then it says unless -- if not stipulated otherwise by this decree, the activities and authorisations stipulated under the law on criminal proceedings are, instead of regular courts of the first instance, conducted by County Military Courts. Now I'm going to skip the second instance regular courts and go on to the only thing that's interesting for my question. That is to say, the organs of the interior authorise persons of security departments of the armed forces. Internal affairs conducted by authorised persons of security departments of armed forces. Now, stay with that text and I'll ask you the question. But Mrs. Alaburic asked you whether the internal affairs organ was in charge of collecting evidence necessary for the attorney to decide whether he's going to accept the proceedings and charges or reject them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection to make. I wasn't looking at the English transcript, but I certainly didn't ask the witness questions of the internal affairs organ, because in response to my question on -- regarding this article read out by Ms. Nozica, he said that the security organ of the armed forces, which pursuant to that article, should conduct the affairs that the internal affairs deals with generally.
