utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said Mijo Bozic, did you mean Kreso?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, in this instance I meant Mijo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to Vares, then I'm sure you're talking about Kresimir Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I don't really have time to argue on this particular point. Where was Mr. Kresimir Bozic, then? Let's start with him. What was his position or function on the 21st of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an operative in the brigade -- in the Bobovac Brigade command, and he was familiar with the situation in Vares and he was familiar with the position of the Bobovac Brigade and he knew everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm setting this up in specific questions to something that I'm going to get to in a moment that has been asked, but I want to get some basic facts established. Can you give us any assistance as to why Mario Bradara was named commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade -- I don't think we need to go there but that is shown in Exhibit P 06000. Do you have any information as to why Mr. Bradara was named as commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade the day before the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he was appointed on the eve of the attack, I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, he's one of your immediate commanders. You were the operative group commander and Mr. Bradara is being appointed as the brigade commander immediately subordinate to you. You don't know why he was named to that position just the day before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why one day before, but I know in general terms why he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the events in the area of Kiseljak when I arrived in Kiseljak, for some reason there was some objections to some -- to his work and whatnot, and he withdrew from that position. And for a long time after that the office was discharged by the deputy commander Mario Bradara. So it was only logical for the position to be permanently filled and for Mario Bradara to be named.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just move on then to this specific question. Can you tell us exactly when, as best you can help us these years later, exactly when Emil Harah was relieved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sent on holiday leave on the 24th pursuant to Colonel Blaskic's instructions, and he returned to his duties after that. But I don't know exactly when after that he was relieved. I believe it was later, but I can't tell you exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you absolutely sure, sir, that Mr. Harah was not relieved on the 22nd of October, the day before the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emil Harah, one day before the attack relieved?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure of that because on that day I found him there and I treated him as the brigade commander, that was my attitude towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at Exhibit 6000, 6000 -- no, I'm sorry, my apologies. I'm trying to go too fast. 10329. 6000 was the appointment of Mr. Bradara, that's the document we were referring to a moment ago, 10329. It is part -- it was part of the larger bundle, and if you will turn in that what's been handed to you a couple of pages down, sir, there is a letter dated the 22nd of October, 1993, and I'm not going to take the time to read the entire letter, but as I -- if I can fairly summarize the letter and if I say if I do it incorrectly, I'm sure I'll be corrected. Mr. Harah comes on the 22nd of October with this letter and says basically, I'm not fit to take on these responsibilities. I can't carry out current operations. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the last paragraph: "Commander, I only ask you for understanding because in such a difficult psychological state my current abilities for leading and commanding are not sufficient enough for the situation," et cetera. And leads me back to the question I put to you, sir: Are you sure that Mr. Harah was not, in fact, relieved on the 22nd of October or - or - are you telling the Chamber that despite what Mr. Harah told you on the 22nd you left him in command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that conversation with him. I told him, Very well, if you're under a lot of pressure the way you explained to me, I'm here now, I'll protect you from that pressure, I will relieve that pressure, and may we then continue working together. He said, Very well then. In that case I can continue if you're here and if you guarantee that I will be protected and that I can go on working normally. I said, Okay, I'm here. If there's any problem, tell me, I'll intervene, because - I apologise - Because in such a situation, it was not reasonable and sensible to remove a commander who had most information, who knew a lot, and who represented a point of authority for the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was a reference this morning to a rule of the Tribunal, and I must put my case to you while you're here in The Hague. And in connection with the relief of Mr. Harah, his removal at the time, isn't it correct, sir, that Mr. Harah wanted to be relieved, and you knew this because he did not want to have anything to do with what was going to happen in the next day or two?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I would object. I would like to remind my learned friend Scott that we have a statement issued by a protected witness. At this moment I don't know the number of that statement. The Trial Chamber is still considering whether to admit this statement into evidence according to 92 bis Rule. In that document we have a detailed description of what was going on with Mr. Emil Harah. And I believe all these questions about his possible relief before the 24th of October, 1993, are totally contrary to the document that I am speaking about and that Mr. Scott is certainly familiar with. I would kindly ask Mr. Scott to provide the integral information to the Trial Chamber and to present that statement that I'm talking about and put questions to the witness within this context, because now he's asking him questions that are not corroborated by any context, and the witness has never told the Trial Chamber that Emil Harah was removed before the 24th of October. We have established without any doubt that Mr. Emil Harah prepared a plan of surveillance, that this was carried out on the 22nd, and that they embarked on the operation on the 23rd or the 24th. If anybody can help with resolution to this dilemma, I would be very glad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if Mr. Scott could just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you turn off your microphone, please. Mr. Scott refers to a Rule of the Tribunal and says he must put his case to the witness while he's in The Hague. The only Rule that Mr. Scott can be referring to is Rule 90(H)(ii) which has no application to Mr. Scott while he's standing on his feet. That's a rule relating to cross-examination. Mr. Scott calls this witness, what he elicits from this witness in the course of evidence in chief is his choice. What he asks about, he asks about; what he doesn't, he doesn't. He cannot then in re-examination rely on Rule 90(H)(ii) as some sort of door he can go through in asking questions. He must rigorously stick to matters arising out of cross-examination, and that rule is for us when we're cross-examining Prosecution witnesses and for Mr. Scott and his colleagues if they come to cross-examine Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please remind us of the question put during cross-examination that was related to Mr. Emil Harah, and once you've done that you may put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and with assistance from counsel, just leaving the page, we're just losing it, counsel indeed said there were questions about Emil Harah, what his role was, that he was involved on the 22nd and the 23rd, that he was involved in surveillance, on the planning on the 22nd and involved in the operations on the 23rd and those were elicited, counsel just said so, on cross-examination, and that's what I am responding to. As to the Rule 90(H), if I misstate it, I apologise for that. In principle, there's a general concept, I agree the rule is stated in the context of cross-examination, I absolutely fully agree. But I think it is also fair, while the witness is here, that there be no doubt about the Prosecution's position on this matter, and I simply made a reference to the general principle, but be that as it may I don't want to get bogged down in that. I just simply wanted to confirm with this witness, in light of the documents that I've been showing to him and in light of the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that -- one of the reasons, and you know that, that Mr. Harah came to you on the 22nd is that he did not want to be involved in these matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just an intervention. It is not true that Mr. Harah sought the witness on the 22nd. The witness arrived in Vares, where Mr. Harah was to be found. So it was the other way around. It was not Mr. Harah who came to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor has just put a question to you. Please give an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't agree with this statement because this referred to the general situation because the BiH army had attacked Vares, broke the lines, and he did not have a solution. He didn't know how to fend this. This referred to the general situation, the survival of Vares, neither him nor I were in a position to know what would happen the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the same way, sir, I put to you not only was the one Exhibit P 06038, which is the one report you say you did not send, it was fabricated later to give you cover as if you had been in Kiseljak at the time. And I put it to you that a number of other documents, including documents attributed to Mr. Harah were also fabricated as part of the cover-up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I would really like to know whether the Prosecutor is now trying to turn this witness into a hostile witness, that would be some sort of an explanation for the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me, I would just like to say this: This is a question that doesn't make sense. If the Prosecutor if now claiming that there are other forged documents, we should see them all. This is an argument put forth by the Prosecution, not a question. This is making the witness answer questions with -- which are very imprecise. What documents is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reference is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go to 6020. I believe this was actually even raised --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't have total recall of the exact page and line number where a particular question was put, but I believe this question was even raised during one of the cross-examinations specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have Exhibit 6020, without going into all the details about it, but there is an indication, there is a suggestion, that this document is -- was fabricated, that it was not prepared, signed, or sent by Mr. Harah. Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question. I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is information that this document is a fabricated document, that it was not prepared, signed, or transmitted by Mr. Harah. And can you either confirm that or if you don't know, you can say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any fabrication or forgery. I don't know that I have ever seen this document, but I know that I gave instructions to forward the information that was available. I can't tell you anything more concrete about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really apologise, but I believe that this is in the interests of justice at this moment. I've asked the witness about this document, the witness answered about this document. He never said what he has just told my learned friend Scott. I really believe that it would be a good thing to clarify all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the -- Your Honour, again, I'm trying to save as much time as possible. It's clear that there's been questions in cross-examination about this document, counsel just indicated so, questions about Mr. Harah's role, questions about what he did or didn't do around these days, and the Chamber's aware of certain other evidence in the case. And I believe that I should -- if the Chamber tells me not to, I won't, but that that information should be put to the witness, and it -- these issues were specifically raised during cross-examination. If the Chamber tells me not to pursue it, then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you're saying that according to you this is a fabricated document. On what basis can you say this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm reluctant to say in front of the witness because it's other evidence that's before the Chamber. I can tell the Chamber -- I would be happy to go into the Chamber when we don't have the witness present. I think everyone in the courtroom is aware of the evidence I'm referring to -- well, most people. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, we have time -- time is short, time is very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The question, Your Honour, is only whether I have a reasonable basis for putting the question to the witness. I assure the Chamber I do. When the time comes to review the related evidence, I'm sure if I'm wrong that will be made very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn to the topic, because we only have a few minutes left, these HVO units that you asked about -- that you were asked about in the Kiseljak area. And basically, if I can -- again, if I'm allowed to paraphrase or summarize, you were asked whether you had a good relationship with the special units, did you trust these units, that is, the Maturice, the Apostoli, it was also suggested to you that the behaviour of the Kiseljak HVO area units perhaps improved after you returned to the area in the spring of 1993 and that -- either it was said explicitly or perhaps the inference was that given that it may have been reasonable for your superiors to believe that those units had been brought under control. Now, sir, in your -- when you pled guilty and when you told the Judges in your case what was true, you had indicated, sir, it's in the statement, that you knew that these units and these commanders Como, Ljoljo, the others had been involved in previous misconduct. Sir, in terms of the Kiseljak unit, the problem with any contrary position is we have the judgements from the Kordic and we have the judgements from the Blaskic case which says that there were extensive crimes committed in the Kiseljak area by the HVO during the time April, May, June 1993 and you were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection, a short objection. The introduction to this question refers to the time when this witness was appointed head of the OG, and after some time established control over the units in his territory, whereas the rest of the question, after referring to the plea agreement, refers to the period preceding that. I believe that this is trying to entrap the witness and put in question the trust of his unit after he had established control over them because of the events that preceded that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you will look, please, at paragraph 15 of the factual basis and paragraph 19 of the factual basis, I think you'll see to the contrary. Again, I'm not going to take the time to read all that -- well, I guess I have to, at least in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Paragraph 15: "At all times relevant to the amended indictment, including on 21 October, 1993, and following, EA knew that HVO units under his command, including the Maturice and the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade, had participated in several earlier operations against Bosnian Muslim villages in Kiseljak municipality and committed crimes against Bosnian Muslims, including murder, rape, destruction of property, arbitrary arrest, and physical assault. These units included, among others, Como, Firga, Ljoljo," and we talked about the specific instances of some conduct by Mr. Firga and Mr. Como. In paragraph 19 says and this witness agreed to it: "EA was aware that by ordering HVO commanders and soldiers under his command and subordinate to him to attack Stupni Do and Bogos Hill and to round up and detain military-aged Muslim men in Vares town there was a substantial likelihood that the crimes charged in the amended indictment would be committed and nonetheless gave such orders in violation of ICTY Statute Article 7(1)." That's what he says and that's what he says he had knowledge of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in paragraph 15 there is precisely what I said, that this refers to previous operations. It says, "several operations." And second of all, something that my colleagues here have already highlighted, I believe that the fact that this witness entered a plea agreement as a condition for a settlement with this Prosecution cannot be evidence or proof in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The statement that he signed and presented to the Judges is true, Your Honour, just like any other statement of a witness, except this one is confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your question? What is your question --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, please wait. At paragraph 15 of his statement, the witness acknowledged that crimes had been committed in villages, in several villages, in Kiseljak municipality. That's it --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but it says in previous operations, meaning when he was not leading those units. That's the first thing. Second of all, it is not the witness's statement, but his plea agreement with the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We get the point. Please put your question, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the question was, after this was: That's correct, isn't it? And so when you say that, you know, you had a trusting relationship with these units and that they weren't, in fact, cleaned up, in fact you knew that these units had a serious problem with misconduct; correct? And we have the Blaskic and the Kordic judgements to prove it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will agree with you. I signed this, I knew that these units had participated in some unlawful and illegal things. I'm talking about both the units and the commanders, and as what I knew about the individuals, I indicated that and I signed it. There's nothing ambiguous here for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm moving on to back in the village of Vares. We're now moving from Stupni Do to Vares and we only have just a couple of minutes left. But again, there's been all sorts of questions and discussion about the isolation of Pejcinovic, Duznovic, and Gavran because they were obstructing the planned activities. Again, could you just assist us, please, and assist the Judges once and for all if you can, exactly what were they doing that was being called obstruction, on the basis of which they were detained, arrested, held, whatever you want to call it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the operations, before my arrival in Vares, I will give you an example. Contrary to all orders by Petkovic, Blaskic, and myself, they released a certain number of militarily able-bodied, and let them go to Herzegovina, which dwindled the military potential for the defence of the city of Vares. After that you saw a number of remarks in Emil Harah's letter. And on the day of the operation I was informed that this had been putting pressure on Mr. Emil Harah and that they personally intervened in the cases of bringing in certain military conscripts, which was done selectively according to their own criteria and what was implied was private links and private businesses that they had with these persons. All this had a negative impact on the mood among the HVO troops, and I was even afraid that there might be an uprisal, because I had information that they were prepared to use their own security service, so to call it, in order to protect themselves and the people that they were in favour of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me come back to that if I have time. But these questions that you've raised about the political -- the HVO political leadership in Vares, this is something -- was this knowledge, were these situations and alleged activities that were known prior to the 22nd of October, or had this all developed over night, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was dissatisfaction with the work of these people prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when you were talking to General Petkovic on the 21st and when the decision was made to send you to Vares through Serb territory, is that something that you and Mr. Petkovic discussed, that there had been -- there was these known -- supposedly known problems of the political leadership in Vares and what should be done about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection to the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you're starting to -- you're starting to raise objections that do not make any sense. The Prosecution is putting questions about the isolation of a number of individuals. Where is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Duty is to intervene if the Prosecutor doesn't put questions in keeping with what the witness has said already. The Prosecutor says that on the 22nd pursuant to a decision he was sent to Vares, I would like to remind you that this witness has stated here that him and General Petkovic agreed together that it would be best for him to go to Vares in order to calm the situation down. So this was not a decision for him to go but a joint decision, an agreement on the part of the two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's a statement by Mr. Petkovic that says: "I sent EA" -- It's in one of the documents if you look. "I sent EA to Stupni Do." But we'll come back to that in the future, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir -- well, again, it's a reference, but I agree, Your Honour, I apologise. Let me just look at my notes and see what I will touch on the last two, three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just get an answer to the question, sir, so these -- these alleged problems with the political leadership in Vares had been known. So my question to you: Before you left Kiseljak early on the morning of the 22nd, you know, we had heard about 3.00 in the morning and then you got there and then you called back Petkovic at 6.00 and said we arrived okay, you sent a message. Before you left, had you discussed with General Petkovic the fact that the political leadership -- the HVO leadership in Vares was somehow problematic and what should be done when you got to Vares?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about that, and this was stated by General Petkovic. He said that they wouldn't listen and they put themself in the situation that they were in. And as for the instructions with regard to them, I did not receive any from General Petkovic, no concrete instructions to take specific measures with regard to these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, I'm going to have to try to encapsulate a bunch of questions into one or two and I'll try to do that as best I can and we won't be able to get through all the documents of course. You've told us since you began your testimony that a high HVO priority around this time was to conduct a breakthrough operation, if you will, to open the Kiseljak-Busovaca corridor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as part of that operation, would that have involved -- would that operation have any success, possibility of success, can you confirm to the Judges that it would have to involve the Ban Jelacic Brigade, the Maturice and Apostoli?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we might have time for one more document if you look at 6425, please. If you have 6425, please, this is, again, an order, communication in any event, on the 4th of November, 1993, from General Petkovic. And number 1, item number 1 says: "Kiseljak OG 2 command, Operative Group command carries out an offensive combat activity in the Vitez military district area of responsibility, Kiseljak-Busovaca. Task to establish a corridor between the Croatian enclaves of Kiseljak and Busovaca. 3, deployment of forces, troops of the -" excuse me, it's getting late - "Ban Jelacic Brigade, the Maturice, the Apostoli shall be deployed in realization of the offensive combat operation." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS EA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell -- my last question, I hope. Can you tell the Judges again, make it very clear as much as you can, what would have been the effect on that operation and the use of those forces if a bona fide serious investigation had been conducted at that time and if the commanders of those units had been detained or arrested? How would it have affected this high-priority HVO operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An objection. The witness is asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the situation within the unit or within the units and given the solidarity of the troops towards each other that I was familiar with, I believe that a major pressure that would have been put on a number of commanders or troops to exclude them from the unit would have resulted in -- in the collapse of that unit, and those units would not be fit for use in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to, under the circumstances, I know what they are, but nonetheless I want to thank you for coming to The Hague again and giving your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I also want to thank the Chamber. I know we've gone a couple minutes over. I appreciate that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before we end today, I would like to remind the Defence that they have to respond at the latest tonight to two motions, request for an addition to the list 65 ter and to -- five -- an addition to five lists, 65 ter. So you have to answer at least by tonight because the Trial Chamber has to render a decision tomorrow, in view of the witness that will come to testify next week. Sir, thank you very much for coming to testify. Thank you for having testified for at least -- well, two weeks because you have been testifying for two weeks. And on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you very much. You raised your hand. You wanted to say something? Please be brief because we're late already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you with regard to the Trial Chamber's decision to ban me from contacting people in the Detention Unit to lift that ban. There is no reason for the ban to be on. I would like to talk to some people and I really don't know when will I have the next occasion to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would object to that. The gentleman had indicated that during his plea and while he was preparing for plea he had contacts with others in order to look at documents which were not privy to him. And I do object to that. I don't think he should be in a position where he's influencing others to do exactly what he was doing here today and in the course of pleading out, making his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will decide on that question this afternoon, so if we grant the decision we will let know the establishment where you are held; and if the decision is contrary, if your request is not granted, then we will not inform the Detention Unit. And I thank you very much. Thank you very much, Ms. Kosta, for having been here for almost two weeks. The session is ended. Thank you.
